body.statement: The bounded-score and nondegeneracy conditions imply \(\sqrt B(\widehat\tau_B-\bar\tau_B)/\sqrt{V_B}\Rightarrow N(0,1)\). Conditional on the denominator law \(\widehat W_B-W_B\xrightarrow{p}0\) and blockwise conservativeness \(b_{Bj}\ge\sigma_{Bj}^2\) for every \(B,j\), one has \(W_B\ge V_B\) and \(\liminf_{B\to\infty}\Pr\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}\ge1-\alpha\). If \(W_B\to W<\infty\), coverage converges to \(2\Phi(z_\alpha\sqrt{W/V})-1\); if \(W_B-V_B\to0\), the feasible studentized statistic converges to \(N(0,1)\).
body.justification: Expected conservativeness alone does not imply coverage; this theorem supplies the correct \(B^{-1/2}\) standard-error scaling and the missing denominator law.
body.gap: \cite{LiDing2017FPCLT} supplies numerator finite-population central limit theory and \cite{HarshawMiddletonSavje2026} supplies quadratic bound-estimator consistency conditions, but neither composes an all-degree observable bound with conservative studentization.
body.consumer: It licenses asymptotic Wald inference for genuinely independent replicated binary exposure blocks using the realized higher-order lookup tables.
body.proof_tex:
All expectations, variances, probabilities, and convergence statements below are under the row-specific randomization law. The potential-outcome schedules remain fixed, so the only randomness is assignment.

For \(1\le j\le B\), define the centered block score
\[
 Y_{Bj}:=X_{Bj}-\tau_{Bj},
 \qquad
 s_B^2:=\sum_{j=1}^B\sigma_{Bj}^2=B V_B.
 \tag{1}
\]
The equality \(s_B^2=B V_B\) is the definition of \(V_B\). By the definition \(\tau_{Bj}=\mathbb E X_{Bj}\), one has \(\mathbb E Y_{Bj}=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_{Bj})=\sigma_{Bj}^2\). Assumption~\texttt{ass:block-independence} implies that the variables \(Y_{B1},\ldots,Y_{BB}\) are independent. Assumption~\texttt{ass:uniform-score-bound} and Jensen's inequality give
\[
 |\tau_{Bj}|=|\mathbb E X_{Bj}|
 \le \mathbb E|X_{Bj}|\le M,
 \qquad
 |Y_{Bj}|\le |X_{Bj}|+|\tau_{Bj}|\le2M.
 \tag{2}
\]
Assumption~\texttt{ass:nondegenerate-average-variance} states that \(V_B\to V>0\). Hence, for all sufficiently large \(B\),
\[
 V_B\ge V/2,
 \qquad
 s_B^2=B V_B\ge BV/2\longrightarrow\infty.
 \tag{3}
\]
Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Equations (2)--(3) imply \(2M\le\varepsilon s_B\) for every sufficiently large \(B\). For those rows every Lindeberg indicator vanishes, and therefore
\[
 \frac1{s_B^2}\sum_{j=1}^B
 \mathbb E\!\left[Y_{Bj}^2
 \mathbf 1\{|Y_{Bj}|>\varepsilon s_B\}\right]=0.
 \tag{4}
\]
Thus the primitive boundedness and variance conditions have derived, rather than assumed, the Lindeberg condition. Applying Lemma~\texttt{lem:lindeberg-feller-independent-array} to (1)--(4) yields
\[
 \frac{\sum_{j=1}^B Y_{Bj}}{s_B}\Rightarrow N(0,1).
 \tag{5}
\]
The definitions of \(\widehat\tau_B\), \(\bar\tau_B\), and \(s_B\) turn (5) into
\[
 T_B:=\frac{\sqrt B(\widehat\tau_B-\bar\tau_B)}{\sqrt{V_B}}
 =\frac{\sum_{j=1}^B(X_{Bj}-\tau_{Bj})}{\sqrt{B V_B}}
 \Rightarrow N(0,1).
 \tag{6}
\]
This proves the asserted design-based central limit theorem.

We next study the denominator. By Assumption~\texttt{ass:block-conservativeness} and the definitions of \(W_B\) and \(V_B\),
\[
 W_B-V_B
 =\frac1B\sum_{j=1}^B(b_{Bj}-\sigma_{Bj}^2)\ge0.
 \tag{7}
\]
For every sufficiently large \(B\), define
\[
 R_B:=\frac{\max(\widehat W_B,0)}{V_B};
 \tag{8}
\]
this division is legitimate by (3). Assumption~\texttt{ass:bound-lln} says \(\widehat W_B-W_B=o_p(1)\). For any fixed \(\eta\in(0,1)\), equations (3) and (7) imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr(R_B<1-\eta)
 &\le \Pr\!\left(\frac{\widehat W_B}{V_B}<1-\eta\right)\\
 &\le \Pr\!\left(|\widehat W_B-W_B|>\eta V_B\right)\\
 &\le \Pr\!\left(|\widehat W_B-W_B|>\eta V/2\right)
 \longrightarrow0.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{9}
\]
The first inequality uses \(\max(\widehat W_B,0)\ge\widehat W_B\), and the second uses \(W_B/V_B\ge1\) from (7).

By Definition~\texttt{def:wald-interval}, equations (6) and (8) give the exact event identity
\[
 \{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
 =\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{R_B}\}.
 \tag{10}
\]
Here \(z_\alpha>0\) because \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Combining (9)--(10), for every \(\eta\in(0,1)\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \liminf_{B\to\infty}\Pr\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
 &\ge \lim_{B\to\infty}
 \Pr\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{1-\eta}\}\\
 &=2\Phi\!\left(z_\alpha\sqrt{1-\eta}\right)-1.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{11}
\]
The equality follows from (6), since the normal law assigns zero probability to the two boundary points. Letting \(\eta\downarrow0\), continuity of \(\Phi\) and the definition \(z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)\) show that the right side of (11) tends to
\[
 2\Phi(z_\alpha)-1=1-\alpha.
 \tag{12}
\]
This proves the conservative coverage assertion without requiring \(W_B\) to converge.

Suppose now that \(W_B\to W<\infty\). Taking limits in (7) and using \(V_B\to V\) gives \(W\ge V>0\). The denominator law then gives \(\widehat W_B\xrightarrow{p}W\), so truncation is inactive with probability tending to one and
\[
 R_B\xrightarrow{p}r:=W/V\ge1.
 \tag{13}
\]
Fix \(\delta\in(0,r)\). Outside an event whose probability tends to zero, \(r-\delta\le R_B\le r+\delta\); hence
\[
 \Pr\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{r-\delta}\}-o(1)
 \le \Pr\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
 \le \Pr\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{r+\delta}\}+o(1).
 \tag{14}
\]
Apply (6) to the two fixed thresholds in (14) and then let \(\delta\downarrow0\). Continuity of \(\Phi\) gives
\[
 \Pr\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
 \longrightarrow
 2\Phi(z_\alpha\sqrt r)-1
 =2\Phi\!\left(z_\alpha\sqrt{W/V}\right)-1.
 \tag{15}
\]

Finally, assume \(W_B-V_B\to0\). Together with the denominator law and \(V_B\to V>0\), this gives
\[
 \frac{\widehat W_B}{V_B}-1
 =\frac{\widehat W_B-W_B}{V_B}
  +\frac{W_B-V_B}{V_B}
 \xrightarrow{p}0,
 \qquad R_B\xrightarrow{p}1.
 \tag{16}
\]
In particular, \(\Pr(\widehat W_B>0)\to1\). Define the feasible statistic on this event by
\[
 U_B:=\frac{\sqrt B(\widehat\tau_B-\bar\tau_B)}
 {\sqrt{\max(\widehat W_B,0)}}=\frac{T_B}{\sqrt{R_B}},
 \tag{17}
\]
and assign it any fixed value on the event where the denominator is zero. Convergence (6) makes \(T_B\) tight, while (16) gives \(R_B^{-1/2}-1\xrightarrow{p}0\) on an event of probability tending to one. Explicitly, for \(L>0\) and \(\epsilon>0\),
\[
 \Pr\{|U_B-T_B|>\epsilon\}
 \le \Pr\{|T_B|>L\}
 +\Pr\{|R_B^{-1/2}-1|>\epsilon/L\}
 +\Pr(R_B=0).
 \tag{18}
\]
First choose \(L\) large using tightness and then use (16); thus \(U_B-T_B\xrightarrow{p}0\). For any \(x\in\mathbb R\) and \(\epsilon>0\),
\[
 \Pr(T_B\le x-\epsilon)-\Pr(|U_B-T_B|>\epsilon)
 \le\Pr(U_B\le x)
 \le\Pr(T_B\le x+\epsilon)+\Pr(|U_B-T_B|>\epsilon).
 \tag{19}
\]
Equations (6), (18)--(19), followed by \(\epsilon\downarrow0\), prove \(U_B\Rightarrow N(0,1)\).

For an exact finite-support stress check showing why no finite-sample coverage is asserted, fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and choose a rational \(\rho\) with \(0<\rho<\min\{z_\alpha^2,1-\alpha\}\). In a one-block four-atom randomization, let \(X\) be uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\), let \(H\) be an independent Bernoulli variable with success probability \(\rho\), and set \(G=H/\rho\). Then \(\tau=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1=\mathbb E G\), so expected conservativeness holds exactly. Nevertheless, the one-block interval covers zero exactly when \(H=1\), because its radius is zero when \(H=0\) and is \(z_\alpha/\sqrt\rho>1\) when \(H=1\). Its coverage is therefore \(\rho<1-\alpha\). Independent replication of these blocks satisfies the denominator law, so this finite-sample failure is consistent with, and delineates the boundary of, the asymptotic result proved above. \(\square\)
